item.title: Understanding the Types of BPD and Their Connection to Substance Abuse
item.description:
Borderline personality disorder (BPD) affects how individuals experience themselves and relate to the world around them. Seeking relief from the emotional intensity that comes with BPD, individuals sometimes turn to substance abuse as a common coping mechanism. To understand why some people find themselves caught in patterns that they want to escape, we first have to understand the types of BPD and how they intersect with addiction.

There is a relationship between these two struggles that goes beyond a simple cause-and-effect. It reflects deeper questions about identity, managing pain, and a human need for stability. The way BPD manifests can determine not only how someone experiences their internal world, but which substances they turn to, and why. These distinctions are essential to break free from the cycle of emotional dysregulation and addiction.

Four Patterns Common Across the Multiple Types of BPD

Because each person is unique, borderline personality disorder doesn’t present the same way in everyone. Four primary patterns help explain the different ways that BPD manifests. These types of BPD are not meant to box people into categories concretely, but rather, they help us understand the ways emotional dysregulation shows up in real life. By recognizing which patterns resonate most with an individual, Christian counselors can guide treatment and offer hope that recovery is possible.

The discouraged type: This form of BPD often appears in people who seem dependent and seek constant reassurance while struggling with feelings of worthlessness. These individuals may appear passive or submissive in relationships and avoid confrontation, even when it would be healthy.

The impulsive type: Those who manifest this type of BPD often engage in risk-taking behaviors and emotional outbursts without concern for consequences. People who struggle with this form of BPT typically act on every feeling without pausing to consider the outcome, and they chase experiences that provide immediate gratification or distraction from inner emptiness.

The petulant type: This form of BPD involves stubborn negativity and feeling misunderstood, which results in pushing others away by simultaneously fearing abandonment. Individuals struggling with this pattern often feel like victims of their circumstances and may express bitterness or resentment toward those trying to help.

The self-destructive type: This pattern of BPD manifests in harmful behaviors directed inward, which include substance abuse, self-harm, or extreme risk-taking to manage unbearable emotional pain. Individuals of this type are the most visibly concerning. They seem intent on destroying themselves, even though self-harm isn’t about wanting to die. It’s about making internal pain visible.

Each of these patterns reflects a different strategy for managing the emotional dysregulation that is at the heart of BPD. Many individuals display characteristics from multiple types, and patterns can shift over time, so these categories are not considered rigid.

The consistency across these patterns is the intense fear of abandonment, unstable self-image, and difficulty regulating emotions that define the disorder. Adding substance abuse to this already intense struggle starts as an attempt to navigate the emotional turbulence that feels impossible to manage any other way.

Why Substance Abuse Co-Occurs with BPD

The connection between BPD and addiction is not coincidental. Most individuals diagnosed with BPD also struggle with substance use disorders. Because BPD creates an emotionally intense environment, substances often offer temporary relief from these struggles.

An individual experiencing rapid mood swings, chronic feelings of emptiness, and a fear of abandonment turns to alcohol or other substances to quiet the internal chaos. Substances only provide a brief escape from emotions that feel overwhelming and unmanageable.

Self-medication is not the only challenge with substance abuse and BPD. The brain chemistry is changed due to substance use, which can worsen BPD symptoms and create a cycle where each issue amplifies the other. Impulsivity is a core feature of BPD, and it can become more pronounced under the influence of substances, and emotional regulation becomes nearly impossible.

Christian counselors recognize that both conditions require integrated treatment. They emphasize that addressing one only leaves the underlying vulnerabilities untouched. The path to healing requires understanding how these struggles reinforce each other and learning how to cultivate healthier ways to cope with emotional pain. One good place to start is with encouraging Scriptures:

Cast your burden upon the Lord and He will sustain you; He will never allow the righteous to be shaken. – Psalm 55:22, NASB

How Different Types of BPD Influence Substance Use Patterns

A specific pattern of BPD often shapes the relationship an individual has with substances. Impulsive-type individuals engage in binge drinking or experiment with multiple substances, trying to find a thrill and temporary relief from boredom or inner emptiness.

Individuals who struggle with the self-destructive type of BPD may use substances deliberately to harm themselves or engage in dangerous combinations of risky behaviors. They are less concerned with pleasure and more focused on punishing themselves or numbing severe emotional pain.

Individuals who struggle with the discouraged type often use substances to cope with feelings of hopelessness and inadequacy. Using substances becomes an internal coping mechanism to numb the discouraging feelings.

The individual who suffers from the petulant type of BPD faces a more complex dynamic when it comes to substance use. They may engage in substance use in response to a perceived rejection or conflict. The result is a pattern where relationship struggles trigger substance use, which creates more relationship problems.

Christian counselors understand these patterns and can develop treatment approaches that address the specific needs of each individual who struggles with substance use and BPD. The goal is to build healthier ways to manage emotional experiences that made substances feel necessary in the first place.

Still, we are all reminded of Jesus’ words:

“Come to Me, all who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” – Matthew 11:28, NASB

The Path Toward Integrated Healing

Co-occurring BPD and substance abuse recovery requires addressing both conditions simultaneously. If BPD remains untreated, traditional addiction treatment fails because the emotional dysregulation continues to drive the compulsion toward substances.

On the other hand, if BPD is treated without addressing active addiction, the treatment is ineffective because substances interfere with the ability to develop healthy coping strategies. Through integrated treatment, individuals learn to recognize that these conditions exist in relationship to one another and must be addressed together.

Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) has become an effective treatment plan for individuals dealing with both BPD and substance abuse. Through this approach, individuals learn specific skills to manage distress, tolerate stress, and build more effective relationships.

Christian counselors often integrate faith-based perspectives and evidence-based treatments to help clients understand their value in Christ as they develop practical tools to manage symptoms. This process involves learning that emotions do not have to be escaped or numbed. Even intense emotions can be experienced, understood, and regulated in healthy ways.

Finding the Support You Need

The relationship between BPD and substance abuse is a reflection of a human tendency to seek relief from pain through whatever feels available. For treatment to be effective, individuals must understand the different patterns of BPD and how they intersect with addiction.

Each type of BPD – the discouraged, the impulsive, the petulant, or the self-destructive – presents a unique challenge and strength in the recovery process. The consistency is the need for integrated treatment that addresses both the emotional dysregulation involved with BPD and addictive patterns.

Healthy recovery includes building new skills, developing healthier coping mechanisms, and discovering that lasting peace isn’t found by escaping emotions. Instead, you can learn to navigate feelings with grace, support, and God’s Word.

If you or someone you know is facing the complex challenges of BPD and substance abuse, professional support can make a meaningful difference in your recovery. Christian counselors are trained to integrate faith-based encouragement with evidence-based treatment to help you navigate this journey and find lasting recovery.

Reach out to our office and connect with a Christian counselor who can help you take the first step toward integrated care for these struggles.

Reach out to our office and connect with a Christian counselor who can help you take the first step toward integrated care for these struggles.

item.title: Pet Grief in Older Adults: Finding Comfort Through Faith
item.description:
The loss of a pet is devastating at any age, but for older adults, the grief can carry a weight that is hard to understand. After decades of life experiences, most people seem to think that older adults have developed the ability to face grief more easily than the rest of us. The reality is more complex.

When an older adult loses a pet that has been part of their daily lives for many years, they can feel overwhelmed by the grief. If a pet has been their constant companion through retirement, illness, or the loss of a spouse, this loss can be painful and lonely. The good news is that this pain can be an opportunity to lean into the grace of God and know how His comfort will extend to their heart.

The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, NIV

Understanding the Depth of Pet Grief in Older Adults

Culture tells us that some losses aren’t that important. For older adults, this message creates a hard situation when they are devastated by the loss of a pet and question the legitimacy of their pain. Pet loss is often dismissed as something that should be sad but easy to get over. This reflects a deeper assumption about aging and emotional resilience that keeps older adults disconnected from their unique emotional experiences.

Many older adults have connections with their pets that go beyond companionship. Their pets have become part of their daily routine and the reason they get up each morning. Some adults have no one else in their lives, so their furry friends have become the only one who depends on them.

When there are no adult children nearby, and a spouse has passed away, a pet will fill the void and go beyond friendship. These loving pets will create a purpose and show unconditional love. This will create a sense of being needed for the older adult who is now the caregiver for this living creature.

The grief of pet loss can often mimic that of human relationships. The shock of the silence when there is no barking or purring that once resonated creates a lonely silence for the owner. There may be feelings of guilt due to decisions regarding life-ending care. Anger is common as the world continues to be okay, while the pet owner feels devastated. The contradiction of these feelings creates a sense of falling apart, even though they look fine to those around them.

Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted. – Matthew 5:4, NIV

When Grief Feels Overwhelming and Isolating

Pet grief in older adults is often accompanied by isolation. This isolation is a response to well-meaning suggestions that seem hurtful to those who have lost their companion. Some family and friends may suggest getting another pet, but this doesn’t negate the pain they feel about the unique pet they just lost.

These suggestions can create a sense of emotional isolation because others don’t understand how special their pet was. While people often mean well, this message conveys that the pain isn’t worthy of respect. The dismissive attitude of this mindset creates a hidden burden for older adults who are already struggling with multiple losses and health challenges.

The pet that was by their side daily and provided emotional support during difficult times is no longer present, and the grief is being compounded by the feeling that the grief should be hidden. Some older adults feel embarrassed about the depth of their grief and end up isolating themselves and navigating the grieving process in silence.

The practical aspect adds another layer of complexity. The bills for veterinary care, cremation costs, and the physical demands of caring for an ill pet bring with them a level of stress that goes beyond the emotional pain. Adults with fixed incomes or limited mobility often feel like these challenges are impossible to overcome, creating a tangled web of feelings of helplessness, regret, and grief.

Christian counselors understand that this type of complicated grief requires a gentle process. They recognize that the shame associated with pet loss is often the reason older adults dismiss the thought of getting support. As a result, a generation of older adults feels they must process loss and dismiss validation.

Even though I walk through the darkest valley, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me. – Psalm 23:4, NIV

Finding Comfort in Faith During Pet Loss

Faith can offer a unique perspective on pet loss and be a profound comfort during the grieving process. The God who created every creature with purpose and love understands the bonds that older adults form with their companions.

Scripture doesn’t minimize these relationships but rather points to a Creator who values all of His creation. This understanding can encourage older adults to find peace in knowing their grief is acknowledged by a Father who understands.

Prayer can be a powerful tool for processing the complex emotions of pet loss. Unlike human relationships that can come with complications and unfinished business, relationships with pets often represent pure love and acceptance. When this kind of pain is brought to God in prayer, the outcome is an honest expression of loss without the need to justify your feelings to those who may not understand.

It often helps older adults view their role as pet caregivers through a spiritual lens. When a person takes on the responsibility of caring for another living being of God’s creation and shows compassion during illness, it reflects Christian love in action. This is a transformative perspective that can turn feelings of guilt or regret into a recognition of faithful stewardship.

Christian counselors often assist with this situation by encouraging the exploration of faith and its relationship with loss and grief. This process involves acknowledging that love creates vulnerability to pain, but that pain is not meaningless in suffering. In times of loss, the pain becomes an opportunity to experience God’s comfort in new depths. This helps us understand how He connects with us during our grieving process.

Praise be to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those who are in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves receive from God. – 2 Corinthians 1:3-4, NIV

Moving Forward with Hope and Healing

Healing from pet loss doesn’t mean forgetting or minimizing the relationship that was lost. Rather, it involves learning to carry the love and memories forward while allowing space for life to continue. The process often requires patience and recognizing that grief has no predetermined timeline or proper way to unfold.

Some practical steps can help older adults process the grief of losing their furry loved one. By doing these things, grief can be transformed into a special remembrance that can help provide closure for the loss of the relationship. A few ideas are:

  • Plant a garden
  • Create a photo album
  • Donate to an animal shelter
  • Create a memorial space for the pet

Faith communities can also support older adults through pet grief. If a church acknowledges that these losses are just as important as other losses that people experience, then that church community is validating the pain and creating a network of support. There have been some instances of churches finding meaningful ways to honor the role of pets through blessing ceremonies or memorial services.

Christian counselors emphasize that moving forward after pet loss doesn’t mean immediate action or decisions about future pets. The focus is on processing the current loss and allowing God’s comfort to work through the natural grieving process. Some older adults may find peace in opening their hearts to another pet companion, while others feel they need to follow a different healing path.

The journey through pet loss grief can ultimately deepen faith and the understanding of God’s compassion. Many times, these older adults feel closer to God after walking through a hard season of loss through tangibly experiencing His comfort.

“For I know the plans I have for you,” declares the LORD, “plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future.” – Jeremiah 29:11, NIV

Consider Support

Pet grief in older adults reflects a depth of love and connection, demonstrating the capacity for relationship and care. Faith offers comfort and a fresh perspective, allowing older adults to honor their grief and love, finding solace in God’s promise of comfort.

Christian counselors can help them navigate pain through understanding what God says about grief. This allows for a more natural healing process rather than one that is hidden because the loss is culturally less important.

For help with pet loss grief in your area, contact your local Christian counseling services to set up an appointment.

item.title: Teen Anxiety, Virtual Reality, and the Inner World of Teen Boys
item.description:
Teen boys often struggle with anxiety even before they develop a life consumed with social media and virtual reality technology. It begins when they are subjected to the pressure to perform, fit in, and stay strong.

Virtual reality (sometimes called VR), gaming, social spaces, and other immersive worlds are beginning to blur the line between escape and harmful avoidance. Virtual reality can ease or intensify teen anxiety, and parents don’t always know what to look for.

How Virtual Reality Impacts Teen Anxiety

Most teen boys choose to escape through virtual reality because it feels like a safe place where they are in control of their environment. They can win the battles and avoid real-life interactions. Many teens feel as though virtual reality is a relief from the anxiety they struggle with daily.

Within the worlds of this technology, they find structure, clear rules, and feedback that they don’t get in real life. These experiences can lower stress and give their minds a break from the constant worries of grades, friendships, and their future.

The appeal to virtual reality is deeper than just a simple distraction. Virtual reality offers teen boys something that feels like certainty in a world that is constantly shifting beneath their feet. The digital world responds with consistency, even though anxiety makes social situations unpredictable and overwhelming.

In virtual reality, the focus becomes levels to complete, achievements to unlock, and avatars that represent who they wish they could be. This is a sense of mastery that can feel like relief when everyday life leaves them feeling powerless and unseen.

There is a new complexity to the connection between virtual reality and anxiety. Some professionals in clinical settings are now using virtual reality-based therapies to reduce anxiety, teach coping skills, and practice facing fearful situations in a controlled way. However, there is concern that being immersed in heavy digital platforms, such as virtual reality, can intensify depression, addiction-like patterns, and social withdrawal in vulnerable adolescents.

Virtual reality doesn’t create teen anxiety, but it can shape how it is expressed. Teens who spend more time in virtual spaces than in real relationships carry their fears and insecurities with them into virtual reality. Once the headset is on, they have fewer chances to practice in-person problem-solving and emotional regulation. The result is a deepened avoidance that makes ordinary situations feel more overwhelming.

When Virtual Reality Offers Help for Teen Anxiety

The other side of this situation is that mental health professionals are exploring ways to use virtual reality as a tool. There are programs in which teens enter carefully designed virtual environments to practice skills for handling anxiety, managing their thoughts, and calming their bodies. By facing specific fears in a gradual, supported way, the goal is to use virtual reality as a bridge between avoidance and real-life engagement.

While the teen is engaged in this type of treatment, they can:

  • Notice how anxiety feels in their body.
  • Learn and practice breathing and grounding skills while they remain in a stressful scene.
  • Understand that strong emotions rise and fall instead of remaining at a constant peak.

Some teen boys find that the structured practice reduces the sense that anxiety is stronger than they are. They begin to discover they can stay present, make eye contact, and complete complex tasks, even though they are in the middle of anxiety. Under thoughtful and careful guidance, virtual reality can support existing therapies rather than replace them.

Christian counselors incorporate this kind of technology alongside talk therapy, prayer, and Scripture to help anxious teens move toward healing. Reminders like this one in Psalm 4 can help teen boys learn to trust God:

In peace I will both lie down and sleep, For You alone, Lord, have me dwell in safety. – Psalm 4:8, NASB

When Virtual Reality Deepens Isolation in Teen Anxiety

Virtual reality is not therapeutic in every instance. Some teen boys use headsets primarily for gaming or for social platforms that lack built-in safeguards. After long hours online, sleep is crowded out, and exercise, homework, and family time come to a halt. Teens who are already struggling with anxiety become trapped in a pattern that quietly reinforces their fears and keeps them from overcoming anxiety.

These teen boys begin to feel that the only way to be valued is to rely on virtual victories. They often avoid real-life situations that could lead to failure or embarrassment. Real-life school situations, such as stress and bullying, lead to the teen finding a safe place in the headset where the harsh and cruel reality is muted. The result is a growing distance between their everyday life and their online identity.

This shift doesn’t happen overnight. It is a gradual process in which the teen boy who once spent time with friends begins to decline the invitation to hang out. The conversations at dinner become short and sometimes defensive as these teens spend more hours in virtual reality.

What started as a way to unwind becomes a primary means of survival. The virtual world becomes a place where this adolescent feels more connected to himself as real-life relationships become more strained and distant.

When teens become immersed in the virtual reality world, parents may notice irritability when asked to turn off the system, declining grades, or trading sleep for late-night engagement in virtual reality. Another significant sign is that they have withdrawn from friendships. These can indicate that anxiety or sadness is driving the teen to use virtual reality for more than just straightforward enjoyment.

Christian counselors help families slow down and ask honest, gentle questions about why the teen boy feels the need to escape. The goal becomes understanding the pain beneath the use of virtual reality rather than shaming its use.

Walking with Anxious Teen Boys in a Virtual Reality World

Connecting with teen boys in a world of virtual reality requires more than just setting screen time limits. Parents are encouraged to listen patiently, develop wise boundaries, and be willing to enter their world without negating their struggles.

For teen boys who struggle with anxiety, the conversation about virtual reality use can be more effective when focused on their inner experience. Through thoughtful and gentle questions, parents can open a door to talk about shame, fear of failure, or loneliness that some teen boys may not know how to name.

Christian counselors assist families in developing practical plans that will include a healthy routine and carefully chosen virtual reality experiences to support growth rather than increase avoidance. Some treatment plans may include collaboration with mental health providers who specialize in virtual reality-based interventions. This will allow technology to be aligned with therapeutic goals in a faith-based treatment plan.

The process of healing includes developing a stronger sense of who they are beyond the screen. This requires them to identify what they value, what brings them genuine connection, and what helps them feel capable in the real world.

Christian counselors help families focus on rebuilding patterns of engagement to honor the teen, his struggles, and his need for an authentic relationship. The goal is to restore balance and help the team recognize that his anxiety does not define him.

Teen boys struggling with anxiety need to know that their worth is not measured by their performance in games, their social status at school, or their ability to hide how much they worry. Christian counselors help these boys recognize that their identity is grounded in Christ, who sees their hidden fears and invites them to bring their anxious thoughts into the light.

If you’d like to learn more about supporting your teen, connect with this office. A receptionist can tell you more about the counseling services offered.

References:

item.title: What Moral Scrupulosity Feels Like
item.description:
It’s admirable when people strive to be decent and morally upstanding, especially when they are setting an example to others. However, sometimes there is something sinister and overwhelming that drives certain people to be good. Moral scrupulosity is a type of Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) that urges a person to become intensely preoccupied with being a good person.

Sadly, it also causes a person to feel extreme anxiety, guilt, shame, exhaustion, and fear of being exposed as a fraud. It is as if they have a voice in their head constantly criticizing their actions, shining a spotlight on their mistakes, and making their small errors feel like unforgivable sins.

Being a decent person takes effort, and it’s not always easy to make the right choices. However, moral OCD causes intense distortions in a person’s view of themselves. Even a person who has a solid reputation can end up feeling like a moral failure because of the intrusive thoughts that surround moral OCD.

As with all forms of Obsessive Compulsive Disorder, it is possible to treat moral scrupulosity. First, however, you must understand how and to what extent it is affecting you.

Not Just About People-Pleasing

On the surface of things, moral scrupulosity often looks a lot like people-pleasing. People-pleasers need more than the average amount of reassurance from others, and the same is true for those with moral OCD. Both people-pleasers and those with moral scrupulosity try to keep others happy, and both want to be seen as kind, thoughtful, generous, and decent. The difference lies in their inner monologue and motivations.

People-pleasers feel the need to make others happy and to keep the peace in every environment. They will compromise their boundaries, disregard their personal preferences, and allow themselves to be taken advantage of to a degree. However, people pleasers do not experience the same inner monologue and intrusive thoughts as those with OCD. Also, people-pleasing habits greatly differ from OCD compulsions.

Moral scrupulosity hijacks a person’s conscience and takes over their actions. As with other kinds of OCD, there is a voice in their head constantly criticizing and challenging them to do certain things, or ridiculing them for not doing certain things.

For example, something as simple as drinking from a plastic straw can spark internal turmoil for someone with moral OCD. A people-pleaser might feel a twinge of guilt for the environment while sipping from a plastic straw. A person with moral scrupulosity will inwardly berate themselves for hours, framing this simple act as hypocrisy and moral failure.

What Moral Scrupulosity Sounds Like

There are two components to every type of obsessive compulsive disorder: intrusive thoughts and ritualistic or habitual actions. Moral scrupulosity is a ridiculing, criticizing, and sometimes threatening inner voice that spurs panic, fear, anxiety, and shame. It might be an echo of someone you know, or it might take on the quality of your own voice, but more cruel.

You will have thoughts like, “Who do you think you are, pretending to be like this?” or “You are being fake, and everyone will notice.” Sometimes your efforts will be singled out, and you will have thoughts like, “No matter what you do, you will never reach the standards you should,” or “You should have felt worse about that.”

None of these thoughts comes anything close to being positive, encouraging, or uplifting, and only results in you feeling worse about yourself. Most of them will have you questioning your self-worth, and some will cause you to wonder if you are a sociopath, a narcissist, or something worse.

Moral Scrupulosity in Action

Moral OCD mostly exists in your head. As with all OCD, the intrusive thoughts frequently lead to compulsive behavior and ritualistic habits. Many of these habits don’t appear to be obsessive or compulsive, but they are connected to the feelings that come from moral scrupulosity.

Some of the most common habits connected to moral scrupulosity are confessing, apologizing, and seeking reassurance. Feeling constantly guilty or on the verge of moral failure will lead you to scramble in an effort to save your reputation or prove your worth. You might have constant conversations with your spouse, partner, confidante, or pastor about your failures, or you might obsessively journal your fears and anxieties.

With moral OCD, you likely replay conversations over in your head, especially if you hurt someone with your words or were dishonest about something. Even when you feel as if you performed well socially, you still review your words and actions.

You will search for flaws, mistakes, or breaches of social etiquette, which you will use to berate yourself afterwards. These performance reviews become a ritual of sorts after any interaction or conversation you have.

Sometimes you will feel compelled to balance the scales with your actions. For example, in penitence for drinking from a plastic straw, you might donate more money than you can afford to a wildlife rescue fund. Actions like these, while hardly ever practical, become important ways for you to prove your morality and challenge your hypocrisy. They are also a way for you to punish personal wrongdoing and prove that you have leveled up your inner goodness.

Besides having a harsh inner-monitoring system, engaging in costly good deeds, and feeling compelled to confess your wrongdoing constantly, moral scrupulosity also leads to rigid rule-keeping. For you, rules are less about maintaining order or discipline and more about heavy ethics and social purity.

Guidelines become commandments, and failure on your behalf to comply with the code is an intense moral failing that you will struggle to repent from. You will likely also avoid getting involved in anything that feels morally gray or ambiguous. This leads you to pass up certain job opportunities, relationships, or hobbies if they seem like they will lead down a morally dubious path.

Free To Fail

As with all forms of OCD, moral scrupulosity is treatable with certain therapies. Forefront among these is Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP). Recognizing the impact of your thoughts and actions is the start, and from there, you must be willing to feel uncomfortable as your worldview and belief system are challenged.

Recovery from moral OCD can only be gradual. You cannot change intrusive thoughts and compulsive actions overnight, nor would it be healthy if you could. CBT challenges the inner beliefs that surround moral scrupulosity, and ERP exposes you to different thoughts and challenges you to try new actions in response to them.

At first, it is unnerving to replace automatic thoughts like “I am a terrible person” with new thoughts like “Even when I make a mistake, I remain a decent person.” In time, your reflexive thoughts and actions begin to shift, and you will find yourself less preoccupied with your own failures and more focused on your triumphs and breakthroughs.

Somewhere out there, faith exists without fear, and love overrides guilt. Grace is not simply a concept applicable to other people who have earned it. Grace is a force that changes those who are most in need of it and most undeserving of it. Although it might be hard to believe, life does not have to be this difficult forever. Not only are you capable of change, but you are worthy of it.

Dealing with any type of OCD is overwhelming. Simply knowing you have an issue is only the start; now you must get help for it.

We host an online catalog that lists the details of many different counselors, where we hope you will find someone who can help you. If you would prefer to speak with people to arrange a meeting with a counselor, our reception team would love to help you. We hope you will find someone who can help you recover from OCD for good.

The post What Moral Scrupulosity Feels Like appeared first on Tacoma Christian Counseling.

item.title: Faith-Based Counseling Versus Secular Counseling
item.description:
Trying to choose between faith-based counseling and secular therapy? This article may be able to help you decide which approach would best support your needs.

About Counseling

Faith-based counseling, in brief, is a holistic therapeutic approach that balances faith and science by integrating traditional clinical psychology techniques with biblical principles and insights. It sees people as whole beings with biological, psychological, social, and spiritual dimensions. It affirms both the reality of mental health struggles as well as that of the God who is sovereign over them.

Secular counseling, on the other hand, is a neutral therapeutic approach that is rooted in science, evidence-based practices, and psychological theory. It is not anti-religious, but its focus is on treating the person rather than the soul. It facilitates mental and emotional well-being through reducing symptoms, increasing self-awareness, and equipping you with strategies to help you cope with or change challenging aspects of your life.

Most faith-based counselors do not require you to be of the same faith as they are, and will not talk to you about spiritual subjects or incorporate religious practices into your sessions unless you want them to.

Similarities and Differences Between Secular and Faith-Based Counseling

Secular and faith-based counselors both share the same goals of providing support and guidance and helping you achieve good mental health. Both are required to have the same training and qualifications to treat mental health conditions, pass the same licensing exams, use evidence-based techniques, and stay current with research and new treatments.

They do not, however, share the same worldview. Faith-based therapists are able to incorporate a spiritual approach into your counseling sessions if you want them to.

Worldview Differences Between Secular Counseling and Faith-Based Counseling

Faith-based counseling does not discredit the value of science, but it is rooted in a different understanding of truth, identity, and healing. It maintains that secular counseling only addresses part of the picture, failing to recognize the spiritual elements that may need healing as well.

The goals of faith-based counseling extend beyond just mental well-being. They include strengthening your relationship with God, helping you find purpose, exploring forgiveness, and recognizing redemption through faith.

The following are three major worldview differences between the two forms of counseling.

Self versus God Secular counseling is rooted in psychological theory and clinical research. Its goal is to reduce symptoms, foster self-awareness, increase emotional stability, equip you with coping skills to handle or change challenging aspects of your life, and improve day-to-day functioning.

With secular counseling, you are seen as an autonomous being, responsible for your own happiness and identity. The emphasis is on self-reliance and self-directed growth, rather than spiritual transformation or dependence on God.

Faith-based counseling does not separate emotional healing from spiritual reality. It recognizes God’s sovereignty, human limitations, man’s spiritual brokenness and need for spiritual healing, and the importance of a personal relationship with God, the ultimate healer and redeemer. The therapeutic process is seen as a collaborative relationship between counselor and client, working together, while depending on God for deeper healing and transformation.

DSM-5 versus the Bible Secular counseling uses the DSM-5 (the standard classification and diagnostic tool used by mental health professionals in the United States) as its authoritative text on mental health conditions, while faith-based counseling relies on the Bible as its primary authority and the DSM-5 as a supporting framework.

Happiness versus Joy Though the two words are used interchangeably, worldly happiness tends to be a temporary, fleeting, external emotion based on circumstances. Joy is a lasting, internal, spiritual state of contentment rooted in a relationship with God that persists even in the midst of trials and difficult situations.

Secular counseling offers practical, clinical tools aimed at improving happiness through personal empowerment. However, these tools just provide short-term fixes that require constant maintenance.

Faith-based counseling, on the other hand, helps you understand the difference between happiness and true joy, which is a deep and enduring gift from God.

Benefits of Faith-Based Counseling

Focuses on the whole person You don’t have to choose between science and faith. Faith-based counseling focuses on the whole person: body, mind, and spirit. It addresses all components of wellness, including mental, emotional, behavioral, relational, and spiritual.

Respects your faith Faith-based counseling addresses life’s struggles in a way that honors and respects your faith, creating a safe, nonjudgmental space.

Integrates biblical principles with evidence-based strategies Faith-based counselors use the same evidence-based practices as secular counselors, such as eye movement desensitization and processing (EMDR) for trauma, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) for distorted thought patterns, dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) for emotional regulation and relationship issues, and solution-focused interventions for practical change, while integrating biblical principles and insights.

Enhances coping mechanisms Faith-based counseling provides access to spiritual interventions such as prayer and reading Scripture to discuss how they apply to your situation. It helps you deepen your relationship with God, which can help increase resilience during crisis situations.

Helps you find purpose and meaning Faith-based counseling helps you find hope and meaning in your struggles by helping you look at them through a spiritual lens that enables you to see the bigger picture.

Provides effective trauma and grief support Faith-based counseling provides a safe space in which to process pain through the lens of faith, hope, and forgiveness

Considers human sin Faith-based counselors understand the connection between negative thoughts, emotions, and behaviors and the sinful human condition arising from the Fall. It emphasizes the transformative power of God’s grace, redemption, and spiritual rebirth.

Focuses on reconciliation Faith-based counseling guides you toward wholeness in all areas of your life, including restoration of your relationships, using a faith-based lens to address issues.

Encourages community Faith-based counseling encourages community engagement to reduce isolation and overcome social withdrawal. It supports connecting with a like-minded group where you can receive emotional support.

An Example of Integrating Faith with a Standard Technique

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is a standard, evidence-based form of talk therapy. It is based on the premise that our thoughts, feelings, and behavior are interconnected, and how we perceive and interpret a situation tends to determine the way we feel and act.

This idea is common to many major world religions as well, which has led to an adapted version known as Religiously Integrated Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (RCBT) that serves as an alternative for clients who wish to integrate their faith into their mental health treatment.

RCBT follows the same principles and techniques as conventional CBT, but uses tools of your faith to help you change your thinking and enhance cognitive restructuring and behavioral activation. Relevant passages of Scripture, for instance, are used to identify and replace dysfunctional thoughts with more accurate, positive ones aligned with the truths in God’s Word.

How to Decide Between Faith-Based Counseling or Secular Counseling

The best fit depends on your personal beliefs, goals, and needs. Are you just looking for symptom relief, for instance, or do you also want to explore deeper questions of meaning, identity, and spiritual growth?

Faith-based counseling may be the better choice if:

  • Your faith plays a central role in your life, and you want your therapy to align with your biblical views and beliefs.
  • You are looking for a holistic approach that addresses body, mind, and soul.
  • You want to address spiritual questions, doubts, or confusion, alongside your emotional struggles.
  • You would like to have prayer and biblical principles included in the counseling process.

Secular therapy may be a more comfortable fit if:

  • You prefer a neutral, secular environment.
  • You do not want faith integrated into the counseling sessions.
  • You want therapy to be strictly clinical and focused on symptom management, coping skills, cognitive restructuring, emotional regulation, and improved day-to-day functioning.

If you have questions, need more information than this article could provide, or would like to set up an appointment to meet with one of the faith-based counselors in our online directory, please do not hesitate to give our reception team a call. Your first appointment is risk-free.

References:
Ian Day. “Christian Counseling vs. Secular Therapy (Psychotherapy): Tips to Help You Choose the Right Path.” Medi-Share. January 8, 2026. medishare.com/blog/three-key-truths-for-why-christians-should-choose-biblical-counseling.

item.title: Faith-Based Counseling Versus Secular Counseling
item.description:
Trying to choose between faith-based counseling and secular therapy? This article may be able to help you decide which approach would best support your needs.

About Counseling

Faith-based counseling, in brief, is a holistic therapeutic approach that balances faith and science by integrating traditional clinical psychology techniques with biblical principles and insights. It sees people as whole beings with biological, psychological, social, and spiritual dimensions. It affirms both the reality of mental health struggles as well as that of the God who is sovereign over them.

Secular counseling, on the other hand, is a neutral therapeutic approach that is rooted in science, evidence-based practices, and psychological theory. It is not anti-religious, but its focus is on treating the person rather than the soul. It facilitates mental and emotional well-being through reducing symptoms, increasing self-awareness, and equipping you with strategies to help you cope with or change challenging aspects of your life.

Most faith-based counselors do not require you to be of the same faith as they are, and will not talk to you about spiritual subjects or incorporate religious practices into your sessions unless you want them to.

Similarities and Differences Between Secular and Faith-Based Counseling

Secular and faith-based counselors both share the same goals of providing support and guidance and helping you achieve good mental health. Both are required to have the same training and qualifications to treat mental health conditions, pass the same licensing exams, use evidence-based techniques, and stay current with research and new treatments.

They do not, however, share the same worldview. Faith-based therapists are able to incorporate a spiritual approach into your counseling sessions if you want them to.

Worldview Differences Between Secular Counseling and Faith-Based Counseling

Faith-based counseling does not discredit the value of science, but it is rooted in a different understanding of truth, identity, and healing. It maintains that secular counseling only addresses part of the picture, failing to recognize the spiritual elements that may need healing as well.

The goals of faith-based counseling extend beyond just mental well-being. They include strengthening your relationship with God, helping you find purpose, exploring forgiveness, and recognizing redemption through faith.

The following are three major worldview differences between the two forms of counseling.

Self versus God Secular counseling is rooted in psychological theory and clinical research. Its goal is to reduce symptoms, foster self-awareness, increase emotional stability, equip you with coping skills to handle or change challenging aspects of your life, and improve day-to-day functioning.

With secular counseling, you are seen as an autonomous being, responsible for your own happiness and identity. The emphasis is on self-reliance and self-directed growth, rather than spiritual transformation or dependence on God.

Faith-based counseling does not separate emotional healing from spiritual reality. It recognizes God’s sovereignty, human limitations, man’s spiritual brokenness and need for spiritual healing, and the importance of a personal relationship with God, the ultimate healer and redeemer. The therapeutic process is seen as a collaborative relationship between counselor and client, working together, while depending on God for deeper healing and transformation.

DSM-5 versus the Bible Secular counseling uses the DSM-5 (the standard classification and diagnostic tool used by mental health professionals in the United States) as its authoritative text on mental health conditions, while faith-based counseling relies on the Bible as its primary authority and the DSM-5 as a supporting framework.

Happiness versus Joy Though the two words are used interchangeably, worldly happiness tends to be a temporary, fleeting, external emotion based on circumstances. Joy is a lasting, internal, spiritual state of contentment rooted in a relationship with God that persists even in the midst of trials and difficult situations.

Secular counseling offers practical, clinical tools aimed at improving happiness through personal empowerment. However, these tools just provide short-term fixes that require constant maintenance.

Faith-based counseling, on the other hand, helps you understand the difference between happiness and true joy, which is a deep and enduring gift from God.

Benefits of Faith-Based Counseling

Focuses on the whole person You don’t have to choose between science and faith. Faith-based counseling focuses on the whole person: body, mind, and spirit. It addresses all components of wellness, including mental, emotional, behavioral, relational, and spiritual.

Respects your faith Faith-based counseling addresses life’s struggles in a way that honors and respects your faith, creating a safe, nonjudgmental space.

Integrates biblical principles with evidence-based strategies Faith-based counselors use the same evidence-based practices as secular counselors, such as eye movement desensitization and processing (EMDR) for trauma, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) for distorted thought patterns, dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) for emotional regulation and relationship issues, and solution-focused interventions for practical change, while integrating biblical principles and insights.

Enhances coping mechanisms Faith-based counseling provides access to spiritual interventions such as prayer and reading Scripture to discuss how they apply to your situation. It helps you deepen your relationship with God, which can help increase resilience during crisis situations.

Helps you find purpose and meaning Faith-based counseling helps you find hope and meaning in your struggles by helping you look at them through a spiritual lens that enables you to see the bigger picture.

Provides effective trauma and grief support Faith-based counseling provides a safe space in which to process pain through the lens of faith, hope, and forgiveness

Considers human sin Faith-based counselors understand the connection between negative thoughts, emotions, and behaviors and the sinful human condition arising from the Fall. It emphasizes the transformative power of God’s grace, redemption, and spiritual rebirth.

Focuses on reconciliation Faith-based counseling guides you toward wholeness in all areas of your life, including restoration of your relationships, using a faith-based lens to address issues.

Encourages community Faith-based counseling encourages community engagement to reduce isolation and overcome social withdrawal. It supports connecting with a like-minded group where you can receive emotional support.

An Example of Integrating Faith with a Standard Technique

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is a standard, evidence-based form of talk therapy. It is based on the premise that our thoughts, feelings, and behavior are interconnected, and how we perceive and interpret a situation tends to determine the way we feel and act.

This idea is common to many major world religions as well, which has led to an adapted version known as Religiously Integrated Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (RCBT) that serves as an alternative for clients who wish to integrate their faith into their mental health treatment.

RCBT follows the same principles and techniques as conventional CBT, but uses tools of your faith to help you change your thinking and enhance cognitive restructuring and behavioral activation. Relevant passages of Scripture, for instance, are used to identify and replace dysfunctional thoughts with more accurate, positive ones aligned with the truths in God’s Word.

How to Decide Between Faith-Based Counseling or Secular Counseling

The best fit depends on your personal beliefs, goals, and needs. Are you just looking for symptom relief, for instance, or do you also want to explore deeper questions of meaning, identity, and spiritual growth?

Faith-based counseling may be the better choice if:

  • Your faith plays a central role in your life, and you want your therapy to align with your biblical views and beliefs.
  • You are looking for a holistic approach that addresses body, mind, and soul.
  • You want to address spiritual questions, doubts, or confusion, alongside your emotional struggles.
  • You would like to have prayer and biblical principles included in the counseling process.

Secular therapy may be a more comfortable fit if:

  • You prefer a neutral, secular environment.
  • You do not want faith integrated into the counseling sessions.
  • You want therapy to be strictly clinical and focused on symptom management, coping skills, cognitive restructuring, emotional regulation, and improved day-to-day functioning.

If you have questions, need more information than this article could provide, or would like to set up an appointment to meet with one of the faith-based counselors in our online directory, please do not hesitate to give our reception team a call. Your first appointment is risk-free.

References:
Ian Day. “Christian Counseling vs. Secular Therapy (Psychotherapy): Tips to Help You Choose the Right Path.” Medi-Share. January 8, 2026. medishare.com/blog/three-key-truths-for-why-christians-should-choose-biblical-counseling.

item.title: Feeling Trapped in Rush Hour Traffic? Discover How Mental Health Coaching Can Help You Stay Centered
item.description:
Few things remind us of how little control we have as well as rush hour traffic does. No matter how carefully you plan, congestion forces you to wait. It has a way of stealing more than just minutes from your day. It drains energy, patience, and sometimes even the good mood you started your day with. You may find help from mental health coaching.

Sitting behind the wheel, you may feel powerless as the line of cars stretches endlessly ahead. That lack of control can stir frustration, anxiety, and even anger. The thing is, the stress of traffic rarely stays in the car. It follows you into the office, into conversations with loved ones, and into the way you handle challenges later in the day. What begins with brake lights and honking horns ends with irritability and tension elsewhere.

Is it really worth ignoring, then? Mental health coaching is one helpful approach that helps to break that cycle and can keep you centered even when the road feels unpredictable.

The Bigger Problem Behind the Wheel

Traffic stress has a lot to do with the way our minds react to situations we cannot control. When we feel powerless, our bodies respond with tension, racing thoughts, and irritability. In time, this repeated stress response can make us more reactive in other areas of life.

The frustration you feel in traffic is likely the same you get when deadlines pile up or when family responsibilities feel too demanding. Many people fall into habits that make traffic stress even worse. Some examples include:

  • Constantly checking the clock and calculating how late they will be.
  • Replaying arguments or stressful conversations while sitting in the car.
  • Using the commute as a time to prepare mentally for conflict instead of being calm.
  • Letting small irritations, like someone cutting in, feel personal.

All of this only serves the purpose of keeping the stress cycle alive. This is why it would really help if you have a way to replace these responses with healthier ones that leave you calmer and more centered.

Mental Health Coaching for Better Ways to Stay Centered in Traffic

Instead of the usual advice like “take deep breaths,” mental health coaching encourages more creative approaches that fit into real life. Some helpful strategies that can make a surprising difference include:

Create a sensory reset Keep something simple in the car, like a calming scent or a textured object to hold. These small sensory cues remind your body to relax.

Turn the car into a learning space Use the time to listen to podcasts or audiobooks that genuinely interest you. This reframes the commute as personal growth rather than wasted time.

Rehearse calm responses Instead of replaying arguments, practice responding calmly in stressful situations. This builds resilience for challenges outside of traffic.

Set a transition ritual Decide on a short routine when you arrive, such as taking a short break before stepping out of the car. This helps you leave traffic stress behind rather than carry it into your next environment.

That said, trying new mental health habits is always easier when you have guidance. Mental health coaching provides accountability and perspective, helping you see where stress patterns show up and how to replace them with healthier ones.

A coach is there to help you connect the dots between traffic frustration and other areas of life, so you learn to respond differently in situations where control is limited. After a while, this builds a stronger sense of calm that extends far beyond the commute.

Traffic will always be part of modern life, but the way you respond to it doesn’t have to drain your energy. Mental health coaching is a great approach to help you reclaim peace in places where stress usually takes over, and those skills carry into every part of your day.

If you’re ready to talk more about building these centering habits, reach out to one of the mental health coaches listed on this site or call the numbers on the screen. Taking that step is a practical way to bring calm back into your daily drive and block out the mad rush noise.

item.title: Chronic Loneliness and the Quiet Ache of Feeling Unseen
item.description:
Feeling invisible in a room full of people can leave you feeling disoriented. Whether it’s at a family gathering, a church service, or lunch with coworkers, something inside of you feels completely cut off from everyone around you. This isn’t a passing mood or a signal that you need a quiet evening at home. For most individuals, it’s a daily reality of chronic loneliness, even amid a busy schedule and a calendar full of social events.

There are no convenient moments for chronic loneliness to show up, but it is there, quiet and persistent, in places and circumstances that are supposed to feel the opposite of alone. This type of loneliness is difficult to address because it rarely looks like loneliness should. It’s not someone sitting alone with nowhere to go and no one to call.

Chronic loneliness is something different. It often affects people who are engaged, busy, and surrounded by family, church, and community. It is the hidden disconnection they feel underneath all of that activity. The first step in healing is to name it. Then, understanding follows, and healing can begin. Even Scripture encourages people to be honest about their loneliness:

Turn to me and be gracious to me, for I am lonely and afflicted. – Psalm 25:16, ESV

The Silence That Lives Inside a Crowded Room

It doesn’t seem right that it works this way; more people should mean more connections. Sitting in church pews with familiar faces or showing up to social events can still make people feel as though they are strangers in spaces where they should feel at home.

This issue goes far beyond not having people nearby. It includes something hard to name: a persistent sense that no one truly sees you, knows you, or notices if you come undone on the inside. This type of absence is more isolating than physical solitude could ever be.

We have societal expectations that shape this experience in ways we don’t always notice. A prevailing attitude that suggests that if you’re actively involved in a rooted community, especially a faith community, you should be fine. This generates an invisible pressure to perform kindness, even when the inside does not match the outside. People learn to smile, show up, and keep participating while feeling disconnected from the environments that foster belonging.

Christian counselors recognize this pattern before people are ready to acknowledge the loneliness outright. They show up exhausted, emotionally flat, and unsure, while nothing feels like it is working anymore. Proverbs 14 identifies this juxtaposition: “Even in laughter the heart may ache, and the end of joy may be grief.” (Proverbs 14:13, ESV)

What Chronic Loneliness Looks Like Beneath the Surface

Chronic loneliness is not a reflection of how many relationships you have. People can surround you, and you can still experience deep, persistent isolation. It is the distinction that matters, because it shifts the focus away from external circumstances toward the internal experience.

That experience is the quality of connection, the sense of genuinely being known, and the emotional safety that you feel in your relationships. When these elements are absent, a void registers in your body and mind, and it is difficult to ignore. It shows up as a quiet sense that something important is missing, and it is accompanied by emotional numbness.

There are social pressures that shape how you connect with others, and they contribute to this far more than you recognize. Competing values around being self-sufficient, productive, and having things together make it difficult to admit there’s something wrong.

Admitting loneliness is like admitting failure, especially in places of faith, where community has value and expectations. The result is a cycle that is difficult to break because of the avoidance of vulnerability. Pulling back deepens the disconnection that you’re trying to manage quietly, and the outcome is a persistent, unnamed suffering that rarely surfaces until something breaks open. Even in these lonely, broken places, you can hold onto the truth that God is near.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, ESV

What Faith Says About Feeling This Type of Aloneness

God’s Word does not pretend that loneliness is not real. There are many honest prayers in the Bible that come from people who felt utterly isolated, such as prophets, kings in hiding, and disciples scattered by fear. The book of Psalms is filled with raw and unpolished cries that name emptiness and abandonment without any apology or qualification.

This is significant because it reminds us that profound loneliness is not a sign of insufficient faith or spiritual weakness. It is simply a human experience that God never asked anyone to minimize, deny, or quietly push through alone. God has always been acquainted with this kind of grief.

Faith does not offer an immediate answer to the ache, but it brings a genuine presence with it. God entered the human experience through Christ, and that His darkest hour was marked by complete abandonment. This doesn’t remove the pain of loneliness; instead, it gives it a witness. The experience of being unseen has already been brought before God, and He did not look away.

When you can bring your disconnection honestly before God and before a trusted community, something shifts. Christian counselors recognize that the intersection of spiritual and emotional health is central to their work. You cannot address the mind without addressing the spirit and expect it to be a lasting change.

Finding Your Way From Chronic Loneliness To Real Connection

Navigating chronic loneliness is not quick, and it is never linear. It requires that you learn to identify what a genuine connection actually feels like, not what it is supposed to look like from the outside. It is understanding what truly leaves you feeling less invisible and more fully yourself.

This process may include grieving the relationships and environments that were unable to offer that kind of safety. It is no secret that grief and loneliness are closely related. It will take patience and honest self-reflection to begin separating one from the other without losing sight of either.

When you reach out to a counselor, a trusted person in your community, or to God in prayer, that is the hardest and most important step. You can then move directly against the social pressure to handle things privately and maintain the appearance of self-sufficiency. This becomes the beginning of something real.

Christian counselors can help you examine the relational patterns that have kept you isolated and understand where those patterns developed. Then you can begin building toward the kind of connection that actually holds. Faith won’t ask you to be fine. It will ask you to be honest, and in that honesty is the very thing that interrupts the cycle.

Don’t Go Through This Alone

Chronic loneliness in the middle of a full life is a quiet form of pain that rarely announces itself and rarely receives the attention it deserves. This loneliness lives beneath conversations and behind smiles, hidden inside of people who have become quite practiced at looking fine while feeling far away from almost everyone around them. It is real, it matters, and it doesn’t have to remain a permanent aspect of your daily life.

There is nothing about your loneliness that disqualifies you from connection, community, or the nearness of God. He has never stopped moving toward the isolated and unseen. The journey toward connection begins with naming what is actually true. That means deciding to stop carrying what was never designed to be carried alone.

Whether you speak with a Christian counselor, reach out to someone you trust, sit in prayer, or acknowledge the weight of what you’ve been quietly holding, that is the beginning. And every beginning is always worth the step.

If loneliness has become a familiar or persistent part of your daily life, you do not have to face it alone. You can reach out to our office today and talk with our reception team to get started on your journey toward something better.

item.title: The Complexities of Dating Someone with Bipolar Disorder
item.description:
There are two truths to dating someone with bipolar disorder. Firstly, it is an experience that not everyone will be open to, and secondly, it can be one of the deepest, most meaningful experiences of your life. The determining factor is how well equipped you are to handle the intense ups and downs that come with the territory of bipolar disorder.

Dating someone with bipolar disorder requires open communication, clear boundaries, and realistic expectations. You will only manage to do any of these things when you are familiar with the disorder in general and when you understand how and to what degree it affects your partner. Having a romantic partner with bipolar disorder requires you to love them in the specific way they need to be loved, and to guard yourself.

Ups and Downs in the Relationship

Most people have baggage, residual trauma, and insecurities that bring tension and conflict into a relationship. However, people with bipolar disorder have a mood-altering disorder that acts as a magnifying glass to all of their self-doubts and fears. It’s not uncommon for someone with bipolar disorder to either shy away from romantic connections entirely or else enter into them with a lot of trepidation.

It’s impossible to love someone who won’t allow themselves to be loved. Dating someone with bipolar disorder often means having to be more patient than you realized you could be. You should be prepared for the manic and depressive episodes, and the way your loved one seems to change with either one.

It will require a lot of grace. You must anticipate the hurtful things they will say when manic, and try not to take them personally. You must also prepare for the times when they become emotionally distant and shut you out because they are overwhelmed with shame and exhaustion during their depressive spells.

One of the first things you must consider as you begin dating someone with bipolar disorder is how they are handling the disorder. Some people have been diagnosed for years, are receiving treatment, have a good idea about their triggers, and can roughly anticipate the rhythms of the disorder.

If this is the case, you will be much better prepared for the ups and downs because your partner is prepared for them. Communication will be more open, and there will be less shame and embarrassment involved.

However, some people have either not been diagnosed or are not coping well with their diagnosis. They have little regard for treatment and don’t even attempt to help themselves or their loved ones during mania or depression.

It is harder to be romantically involved with people who take this approach to bipolar disorder because you cannot set boundaries as easily, or support them without draining your personal resources. No relationship can survive when one party has a disregard for their own health and their loved one’s happiness, regardless of whatever disorders are at play.

Practical Things You Can Do at the Start of the Relationship

One of the first steps you must take when dating someone with bipolar disorder is to familiarize yourself with the condition. Do as much research on the topic as you can. Ask your partner questions about their experience, but only do so when they are in a stable mood. Show that you are curious, non-judging, and open to learning so that you can better support them.

More important than doing research or even asking questions is listening. Take note each time they open up about their experience, knowing that no website can teach you as accurately as your partner can when it comes to their lived experience. Listen to what they share concerning what their episodes feel like, and what helps and what doesn’t help.

When it’s appropriate and when they are in a stable mood, have a conversation about their triggers and patterns. Try to determine any early warning signs for a manic episode, such as periods of stress or anger. You will have to figure out how best to respond to these triggers, knowing that there’s not necessarily a way to help them avoid an episode. Knowing their triggers is more of a benefit to you, so that you can anticipate what happens next.

When dating someone with bipolar disorder, one of your major roles will be that of caretaker. It is not a constant role. The disorder is not static and changes somewhat regularly. Bipolar disorder is treatable with medication, which brings emotional balance, and therapy, which helps with their long-term outlook. You can help by encouraging treatment, following up about medication, and accompanying them to doctors’ appointments, if they invite you.

Lastly, in the beginning stages of dating someone with bipolar disorder, it is essential to remember to keep your own life intact. Every healthy relationship is made up of two individuals with unique interests, hobbies, responsibilities, and a life outside of the relationship. It’s easy to let the high demands of a relationship like this become consuming. You must maintain a life outside of the relationship, and do so from the start.

Strapping In for the Long Haul

You cannot maintain a successful long-term relationship unless you take care of yourself. Regardless of how well they manage the disorder, being in a relationship with someone with bipolar disorder often means dealing with volatility, caregiver fatigue, and emotional exhaustion. There are several important boundaries you must establish as soon as you see the relationship deepening.

Firstly, it’s important to learn to use ‘I’ statements when establishing boundaries, but also when simply expressing yourself in the relationship. Talk about your experience, your limitations, and your concerns by prefacing statements with “I.” “I feel like I’m the only one making an effort here,” or “I will not tolerate threats, regardless of what episode you are going through,” for example. Establishing boundaries is about protecting yourself, not about changing, shaming, or controlling your partner.

Secondly, never attempt to have important conversations like these during either depressive or manic episodes. Your partner needs to be in a clear frame of mind so that they can fully understand what is being established, with no clouded judgment. You need to be selective about when you have certain discussions when you are dating someone with bipolar disorder.

You must decide and communicate what behavior you will not accept, regardless of whatever episode they are going through. During a manic episode, your partner might say cutting things, accuse you of things you have never done, or become threatening and physically intimidating. They will likely regret everything once the episode passes, but you are never obligated to receive this kind of treatment.

Have an honest conversation about what you will do in the event of them saying hurtful things during mania. Consider having zero tolerance for abusive language, physical aggression, threats, reckless spending, or cheating, all of which commonly happen during manic episodes.

One of the most common areas to affect any relationship, especially in the long term, is finances. People in a manic episode tend to become overly generous and impulsive, and this can cause many financial issues. It’s a good idea to have separate bank accounts for this reason and to refuse their access to your personal funds.

You might also have to consider whether you will help them manage any debts incurred during a manic episode, keeping in mind that you are not obligated to if you have separate accounts.

Lastly, pay attention to your own needs and be generous with yourself. Ensure that you are getting quality sleep, plenty of time with friends, a healthy diet, and enough time alone. While you might not have the same mental health struggles as your partner, your well-being is every bit as important as theirs.

If you are dating someone with bipolar disorder, you could greatly benefit from counseling. You don’t have to go through things alone. We hope that you will be able to find a counselor either by consulting our online catalog or by speaking with someone on our reception team.
